newsitem.title: UK: One rate rise enough to curb UK economy -economist.
newsitem.headline: One rate rise enough to curb UK economy -economist.

text.p: The Bank of England needs to raise interest rates only once more to ease the British economy into a painless "soft landing", a leading British economist said on Friday.
In spite of frenzied high street spending, a soaring pound will inevitably lead to a deterioration in the UK's trade balance next year and slow the economy as a result.

"Domestic demand pressures suggest higher rates may be needed but the strength of the pound points in the opposite direction," said Andrew Sentance, head of the London Business School's Centre for Economic Forecasting.
"As a result, a rise in interest rates to seven percent ...should be sufficient to achieve slower growth next year and keep inflation on target."

The super-strong pound has cut import prices and hit exporters by pushing up their prices. Both factors help ease inflationary pressures. The bad news is that the squeeze inflicted on manufacturers will force the loss of 100,000 jobs, losses, Sentance said.
He said the Bank's monetary policy committee, now free to set rates, could easily raise base rates to seven percent when it meets next week and then sit back.
Base rates have already been nudged up in three quarter-point moves to 6.75 percent since the Labour Party's landslide election win on May 1.

A Reuter poll of 23 London-based economists, released on Thursday, found 16 expect a quarter-point rate rise next week. But most forecast a succession of rate rises, not just one. Sixteen of the 23 saw rates peaking at between 7.5 and 8.25 percent.
Sentance argued that sterling -- already up more than 25 percent in a year -- will hit Britain's terms of trade soon, probably within the next couple of months.

He forecast a small current account surplus this year, but a gaping 10.5 billion pound deficit in 1998. "Over the year ahead, the deterioration in the balance of payments will act as a safety valve for the UK economy."
Millions of British consumers are sitting on a massive 35 billion pounds worth of free shares from building societies which have converted into banks.

But a spiralling pound tempts people to spend their windfalls on foreign holidays and imported consumer goods. Equally, it will encourage manufacturers to switch production away from exports to meet home demand.
Both factors will help to keep a lid on inflation.
If sterling suffered a sustained and sudden tumble -- and on the highly speculative currency markets anything is possible -- a greater burden would fall on interest rates to tighten policy.
But Sentance said the Bank could guide the economy to a soft landing by keeping a close eye on a three-point check list.
First, average earnings and pay deals should be watched to make sure wage inflation is not taking off.

Second, the Bank should be aware that consumer spending is unlikely to slow this year because of the billions of pounds in one-off payments. But as long as consumption does not accelerate further, interest rates need rise no higher than seven percent.
Third, there needs to be clear evidence that the pound is diverting demand overseas.
As for unemployment, Sentance expects 100,000 manufacturing jobs to be lost as the pound forces export prices higher.

But that will be more than offset by opportunities in other parts of the economy. He expects unemployment to hit a trough below 1.5 million and stay there until after the turn of the century. The total was 1.6 million in June.
